chapter: Friars Inn, NORK and Chicago influences
title: White and Black musicians kept apart in Chicago
summary: Ashcraft says white musicians seldom connected with Black bands like Oliver's, with separate unions and Black bands seen as entertainers.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah. That's why I don't, I think that it wasn't until after Bud, Tesh, and the others had heard Louie, or rather heard the Oliver Band, out in the south side, that they really connected the two up. And I'm not too sure they did. They were inclined to separate the white and Negro musicians, partly because the economics of Chicago at that point had the Negro musician either playing on the south side or playing as an entertaining type of band. They used to think of moments as a clown band. And it would be only the rare few of us who were interested in music who realized that Jimmy Nunes wasn't just a funny guy, you see, and that Baby Dodds wasn't being tricky. Because he was consciously entertaining when he went out and played parties. And they had the two separate unions.
